sections.title: Problem, Scope and Requirements (API Rate Limiter)

pages.title: Problem, Scope and Requirements (API Rate Limiter)

items: ==Cap requests== per **client** per **time window**
Protects backends from {red:abuse}, {orange:overload} and {purple:noisy neighbours}
Decision per request: ==allow== or ==reject==, before the backend is touched
Configurable ==rules==: client, endpoint, limit, window
Return **429** with `Retry-After` when rejected
Rule changes go ==live without redeploy==
Example tiers: free 100/min per API key, paid 1,000/min, login 5/min per IP

blocks.note: one rule = client key + endpoint + limit + window

items: Added latency under ==2 ms p99==
Availability ==99.99%== (about 52 min downtime a year)
Eventual consistency is fine: about ==5% overshoot== tolerated
Counters fit in memory: 1 GB, so throughput is the hard part

blocks.title: Never the cause of an outage
blocks.text: The limiter protects the backend, so it must **never** be the thing that takes the API down. A limiter failure must not block healthy traffic.

items: Enforce at the ==edge==: rejected traffic **never reaches** the backend
{green:Local} in-process check first (cheap, no network)
{red:Redis} check second, only when the local check passes
Reject answers ==429== straight from the gateway

rows: One proxy per service to run

blocks.title: Rules to keep
items: Do not trust the client to limit itself
Local check first, Redis second
Limiter must never be the cause of an outage

blocks.title: Default design
blocks.text: Limiter middleware **inside the API gateway**, local check first, shared ==Redis cluster== second, rules pushed by a config service.

sections.title: Token Bucket and Leaky Bucket (API Rate Limiter)

pages.title: Token Bucket and Leaky Bucket (API Rate Limiter)

items: Bucket holds up to ==B== tokens (capacity), refilled at ==R== tokens/s
Each request takes **1 token**; empty bucket means {red:reject} with 429
Allows ==bursts up to B==, then settles to R req/s
Store only ==tokens== and ==last_refill== per key
On request: `tokens = min(B, tokens + (now - last) * R)`
{green:No background timer} needed; refill is computed on demand
State is **2 numbers per key**

lines: ok = s[0] >= 1; s[0] -= ok; return ok
blocks.note: B=10, R=5/s: burst at t=0, then one second later

items: B=10, R=5/s: a burst of ==10 passes instantly==, the 11th is rejected
After that only **5 req/s** are sustained
Leaky bucket = ==FIFO queue of size N== drained at a constant rate
Queue full: new requests are {red:dropped}
Output is **smooth**, but a burst waits in the queue (extra delay)
Old queued requests can ==starve new ones==

rows: pass at once, up to B
queue of up to N requests

blocks.title: Whose clock?
blocks.text: Never use the **client's clock** for refill: it can be skewed or forged. Always use the ==server clock or Redis TIME==.

sections.title: Fixed and Sliding Window Algorithms (API Rate Limiter)

pages.title: Fixed and Sliding Window Algorithms (API Rate Limiter)

items: Key = `client:floor(now/window)`, so every request in one window hits the ==same counter==
Per request: `INCR` the key, and `EXPIRE` it on the first hit
{green:O(1) memory}: one integer per client, the ==simplest== algorithm
Reject once the count passes the limit, e.g. 100/min
Store one ==timestamp per request== in a Redis sorted set
Drop entries older than `now − window`, then count what is left
{green:Exact}: the window moves with every request, no boundary burst
{red:O(N) memory}: a limit of 100 means ==100 entries per client==

blocks.note: timestamps are the score and the member

items: Keeps two fixed-window counters: ==current== and ==previous==
Estimate = `cur + prev × (1 − elapsed fraction)`
Assumes the previous window's requests were spread evenly
{green:O(1) memory}; error ≈ ==0.003%== (Cloudflare's measurement)

blocks.title: Pick the default
blocks.text: Fixed window is cheap but lets ==2× the limit== through at a boundary. Use the ==sliding window counter== unless you need exact counts.

sections.title: Redis-Based Counters and Data Model (API Rate Limiter)

pages.title: Redis-Based Counters and Data Model (API Rate Limiter)

items: Schema: `rl:{client_id}:{rule_id}:{window_start}`
Wrap ==only client_id== in braces: it is the **hash tag**
Redis Cluster hashes the first `{...}` pair only
So all of one client's keys share a ==slot== and one shard
**Fixed window**: `INCR key`, then `EXPIRE key window` on the ==first hit== only
Set ==TTL = 2 × window==: old keys clean themselves up
**Sliding log**: `ZADD` the timestamp, trim old entries, `ZCARD` to count
**Token bucket**: `HSET` tokens and ts on a hash, give the hash a TTL

blocks.note: sliding log (60 s window), then token bucket state

items: Estimate: **10M clients × 2 rules × ~100 B** = ==~2 GB==
Memory is small, so ==throughput== (not memory) sets the shard count
`INCR` and `EXPIRE` as two separate commands
A crash between them leaves a key that ==never expires==
Fix: one atomic Lua call (window 60 s, TTL 120 s):

lines: EVAL "local c=redis.call('INCR',KEYS[1]) if c==1 then redis.call('EXPIRE',KEYS[1],ARGV[1]) end return c" 1 rl:{u42}:api:1735689600 120
blocks.note: INCR and EXPIRE run as one unit

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: One ==hash tag on client_id== keeps a client on one slot; ==TTL = 2 × window== plus an atomic INCR+EXPIRE means no key leaks.

sections.title: Race Conditions and Atomicity (API Rate Limiter)

pages.title: Race Conditions and Atomicity (API Rate Limiter)

items: Limit 100/min is checked by ==50 gateways== at the same time, so reads and writes interleave
A **GET then SET** is two round trips: nothing stops another node from slipping in between
Result: every lost update lets ==one extra request== through; under load the overshoot grows
**Fix 1**: ==INCR== first, then compare the returned value to the limit
INCR is atomic and returns the new count: ==1 round trip==, no gap to race in
Fits ==fixed windows== only; refill and sliding logic need more than one command

lines: n = r.incr(key)  # atomic +1, returns new value
blocks.note: no GET, so nothing to interleave

items: **Fix 2**: a ==Lua script== runs on Redis's single thread; no other command runs mid-script
Script does read, refill, decide, write as one unit: ==1 round trip, about 0.2 ms==
Call it with `EVALSHA sha 1 key B R`; load once with `SCRIPT LOAD` to skip resending the body

lines: local tok = math.min(ARGV[1], (s[1] or ARGV[1]) + (now-(s[2] or now))*ARGV[2]/1000)
if ok then tok = tok-1 end
blocks.note: token bucket: ARGV[1] = B, ARGV[2] = R per second

items: `WATCH key`, read, then `MULTI` ... `EXEC`: EXEC ==aborts== if the key changed since WATCH
This is ==optimistic locking==: on abort the client must retry the whole read-decide-write
Under contention on a hot key, retries pile up and latency climbs

blocks.title: One clock for all nodes
blocks.text: Never read time on the app server and pass it in as ARGV. Clocks drift between nodes, so refill math disagrees. Call ==redis.call('TIME')== inside the script so every node shares **one clock**.

sections.title: Limit Keys and Rules: User, IP, API Key (API Rate Limiter)

pages.title: Limit Keys and Rules: User, IP, API Key (API Rate Limiter)

items: Order: {green:API key} → {blue:user ID} → {orange:IP}
==IP is only the fallback== for anonymous traffic
Rule = (key, endpoint, limit, window), looked up per request
**NAT or office**: many users share one IP, so legit users get blocked
**Attackers rotate IPs**: each new IP gets a fresh limit
Behind a proxy, the socket IP is the proxy, not the client

blocks.title: X-Forwarded-For
items: Trust `X-Forwarded-For` ==only from your own proxies==
Read the client IP from the hop your proxy appended
Anyone else can forge the header and dodge the limit
Check every tier; ==deny if any one tier fails==
Weight expensive calls: spend more tokens per request
With 1,000 tokens/min: 200 searches or 1,000 reads

blocks.title: One global limit for all clients
blocks.text: A single shared limit lets ==one abusive tenant exhaust it for everyone==. Always key the limit **per client** (API key, user or IP).

sections.title: Response Headers and Client Behaviour (API Rate Limiter)

pages.title: Response Headers and Client Behaviour (API Rate Limiter)

items: Reject with ==429 Too Many Requests==
{red:Never 503} (looks like an outage) and {red:never 403} (looks like a permission failure)
Send the headers on every response, so clients can slow down before they hit 429

rows: How long to wait, sent on **429**

items: IETF draft names: `RateLimit-Limit`, `RateLimit-Remaining`, `RateLimit-Reset`
Same three values, no `X-` prefix

blocks.note: free tier, 100 req/min per API key, bucket empty

items: Retry with ==exponential backoff== plus ==full jitter==
`sleep = random(0, min(cap, base × 2^attempt))`
Jitter spreads retries out, so no **synchronized retry storm**
If `Retry-After` is present, wait at least that long

lines: print([min(cap, base * 2**n) for n in range(6)])
print(all(sleep_for(n) <= min(cap, base * 2**n) for n in range(6)))
blocks.note: upper bound of the sleep window per attempt

items: Rejected requests that still count against the limit, so a client can never recover
Retries with no jitter: all clients return in the same second
Using 503 or 403 instead of 429, so clients do not back off

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: ==429 + Retry-After== tells the client when to return. ==Full jitter== keeps 1,000 blocked clients from returning in the same second.

sections.title: Distributed Deployment and Synchronization (API Rate Limiter)

pages.title: Distributed Deployment and Synchronization (API Rate Limiter)

items: ==Exact counts==: every gateway updates one shared counter
Cost: one network hop, about ==0.5 ms== per request
Redis becomes a {red:hot dependency}: 1M req/s peak all lands on it
Fits the budget: under 2 ms p99 added latency
Local counters sync with Redis every ==100 ms==: no hop per request
Overshoot is up to ==nodes × local batch size==
Batching: a gateway ==leases 10 tokens== from Redis, spends them locally
Redis calls drop ==10×== versus one call per request
Worst case held unspent: 50 nodes × 10 tokens = ==500==
10,000/min rule: 500 is 5%, inside the ~5% tolerance
1,000/min rule: 500 is {red:50% overshoot}, ten times too much
Size the lease from the limit: 5% of 1,000 = 50 tokens = ==1 per node==

rows: over by up to nodes × batch

items: Sticky routing: ==hash(client)== puts a client on one node
Local limit is ==exact==, nothing to sync
{red:Node loss} resets its clients' counters to a fresh limit

blocks.title: Limit ÷ node count
blocks.text: 100 limit ÷ 50 nodes = ==2 each==. With uneven load balancing a busy node rejects at 2 while idle nodes waste their share, so clients are blocked **below** the real limit of 100.

sections.title: Failure Modes and Metrics (API Rate Limiter)

pages.title: Failure Modes and Metrics (API Rate Limiter)

items: Limiter must **never** cause an outage, so ==fail-open== is the default
Choose fail-closed per endpoint, e.g. login at 5 req/min per IP
A timed-out call adds up to ==5 ms==, over the 2 ms p99 budget
The timeout only **caps** the worst-case wait
The breaker stops paying it: skipping Redis keeps most requests under 2 ms
{red:Hot key}: one huge client hammers a single Redis shard
Example: 1 client at 20k req/s loads one shard of ~150k ops/s
Fix 1: ==local pre-check== rejects obvious over-limit calls in-process
Fix 2: ==per-key local cache== of the denied state until reset, no Redis call
Node clocks drift, so never read time on the gateway
Read ==Redis TIME== inside the Lua script: one clock for all nodes
Replica failover can lose the last ==1 s== of counters
Accepted overshoot: briefly more requests allowed, within the ~5% tolerance

blocks.note: now in ms from Redis, not from the app server

rows: Spike in rejects = abuse or bad rule
Alert on CPU above 70%, memory near ~250 MB per shard

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: Redis timeout **5 ms**, breaker trips after **5** failures for **10 s**. Fail-open by default, fail-closed on login and payments.

sections.title: Scaling, Trade-offs and Interview Questions (API Rate Limiter)

pages.title: Scaling, Trade-offs and Interview Questions (API Rate Limiter)

items: {green:Shard}: 1M req/s ÷ 150k ops/s ≈ 7, so ==8 masters== sized for the uncached peak
Only the 8 masters hold counters: ==about 250 MB each== (2 GB total)
{blue:Replicate}: 1 replica per master for failover; replicas hold copies, not extra capacity
{orange:Local cache}: 80% fewer Redis calls leaves about ==200k ops/s==
After the cache, 2 shards could carry the load; the other 6 are ==headroom== for spikes and failover
Standard interview answer: ==sliding window counter + Lua script== on Redis
Multi-region: **per-region limits**, async replication between regions
Global limit is ==approximate==; accept the overshoot instead of a cross-region call per request

blocks.title: Split quota by traffic share
items: Paid tier 1,000 req/min across 2 regions
Region A (60% of traffic): 600 req/min
Region B (40% of traffic): 400 req/min
Re-balance the split as traffic shifts
**How do you stop a boundary burst?** Use a ==sliding window counter== (cur + prev × (1 − fraction)) or a ==token bucket==
Why it works: fixed windows reset at a hard edge (100 at 12:00:59 + 100 at 12:01:00); both smooth that edge
**What if Redis dies?** {green:Fail-open} with local fallback limits, {red:alert}, and {red:fail-closed} on sensitive endpoints

blocks.title: Size for the peak, not the cache
blocks.text: Size shards for the ==uncached 1M req/s== peak; treat the 80% cache cut as headroom, never as the reason to run fewer masters.

items: {blue:Token bucket}: capacity ==B==, refill rate ==R== tokens/s, 1 token per request
==Lazy refill==: `tokens = min(B, tokens + (now - last) × R)`, no timer
State is 2 numbers per key; ==burst friendly== up to B
Example: B=10, R=5/s lets 10 pass instantly, then 5 req/s
Time comes from the **server or Redis TIME**, never the client
{purple:Sliding counter}: `est = cur + prev × (1 - fraction)`
Example: 30% into window, prev=84, cur=36 gives 36 + 84×0.7 = ==94.8==
O(1) memory and no boundary burst: the best default balance
Run check, refill and write as one ==Lua script== called by `EVALSHA`
==Hash tag== `{client_id}` keeps all of a client's keys on one slot
==TTL = 2 × window== so idle keys clean themselves up
Use `redis.call('TIME')` inside the script, one clock for all nodes

blocks.note: 1 key, then args B=10, R=5, cost=1; one round trip

items: Reject with ==429== plus `Retry-After: 30` (seconds)
`X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, `X-RateLimit-Reset` (epoch seconds)
Client retries with ==jittered backoff==: `sleep = random(0, min(cap, base × 2^attempt))`

rows: Redis outage must not become an API outage
Skip Redis, use in-memory local limits

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: ==Lua + EVALSHA== for atomic decisions, ==fail-open== by default, and ==jitter== on every client retry.

blocks.q: A fixed-window limiter allows 100 requests per minute. A client sends 100 requests at 12:00:59 and 100 more at 12:01:00. How many are allowed, and does a sliding window counter allow the second batch?
a_bullets: Fixed window: all 200 pass, because the two batches fall in different window keys.
That is 200 requests in about 1 second, double the intended rate (the boundary burst).
Sliding counter at 12:01:00: elapsed fraction is 0, so the estimate is cur + prev × 1 = 0 + 100 = 100.
That already hits the limit, so the second batch is rejected.

blocks.q: Sliding window counter, limit 100. You are 30% into the current window, prev=84 and cur=36. What is the estimate, and is the next request allowed?
a_bullets: 94.8 is below 100, so the request is allowed, and cur becomes 37.
Adding the raw counts (36 + 84 = 120) would wrongly reject it.
The previous window's weight shrinks as the current window ages.

blocks.q: Spot the bug: a fixed-window limiter runs INCR key, and when the result is 1 it runs EXPIRE key 60 as a separate command. What can go wrong and how do you fix it?
a_bullets: If the gateway crashes or the connection drops between the two commands, the key has no TTL.
The counter then never resets, so that client is blocked forever once it reaches the limit.
Fix: run INCR and EXPIRE inside one Lua script via EVALSHA, so they apply together.
Also set TTL = 2 × window so stale keys clean themselves up.
example_code: if n == 1 then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) end

blocks.q: Two gateways each run GET count and both see 99 with a limit of 100. Each then allows the request and runs SET count 100. What is wrong, and what does an atomic INCR change?
a_bullets: Check-then-set race: both read 99 before either writes, so both allow. The count ends at 100 but 101 requests passed.
With atomic INCR, Redis serializes the two calls and returns 100 to one gateway and 101 to the other.
The gateway that gets 101 is over the limit and rejects, so exactly 100 pass.
For token buckets, which need read, refill, decide and write, use a Lua script so the whole sequence is atomic.

blocks.q: Token bucket with B=10 and R=5 tokens/s. It starts empty at t=0. At t=1s a client sends 8 requests at once. How many pass? How many tokens does it hold after sitting idle for 10 s?
a_bullets: Lazy refill at t=1s: tokens = min(10, 0 + 1 × 5) = 5.
So 5 requests pass and 3 are rejected with 429.
After 10 s idle: min(10, 0 + 10 × 5) = min(10, 50) = 10, so the bucket caps at B.
The cap is why bursts are limited to B. Compute time from the server or Redis TIME, never the client's clock.
